The summer I was twelve, my aunt Ilse rebuilt the old wood kiln behind her house in Hesk. Her teacher, Mr. Varga, had fired it for forty years and left her his notes when he died that winter. She relaid the firebox from his own drawings. The first load would hold a tall jar Mr. Osgood had ordered for the mill's hundredth year, in a blue he had picked from a test tile.

We lit it at dawn. Ilse carried in the wood from the shed and watched the fire through the spyhole, and she gave me the firebox to feed, which was my job until dawn came round again. Once, while she ate, I watched the spyhole for her. At dusk Mr. Osgood helped her cover the woodpile with a tarp, and a long story about the mill kept him at our gate till dark.

Near midnight the storm came, hissing on the chimney cap, and the fire began to sink. Ilse read the notes to herself, found where Varga had brought a firing through worse rain by closing the damper halfway and feeding slowly, and set the book aside. 'You'll learn this by feel or not at all,' she said, and left the poker in my hands. I had expected her to follow him exactly for a first firing. I fed it fast and wild, and forgot my fear that Mr. Osgood would take only the blue of his tile.

Two days later we took down the bricked-up door with Mr. Osgood watching. Ash I had stirred up had blown across the jar and melted into the glaze, turning the blue of his tile the color of a frog's back, a strange speckled green. Ilse tapped it with her knuckle, listening for any flaw the eye might miss, a crack under the glaze, and it rang clear. Mr. Osgood laughed until he had to sit down, then paid her double.

He named it the Pickle, and the Pickle has stood in the mill window ever since. Children count its spots through the glass. Whenever I walk past, I catch myself grinning back at it like a fool.

passage:
Every January for thirty-one years, Tomas Brill, a retired signalman, has carried a torch and a pencil notebook into the disused Pellow railway tunnel to count the bats asleep on its walls. In that time the colony has grown, with only the occasional fall, from forty to nearly three hundred, with a smaller winter roost at the old lime kilns in Fennick, half a mile down the valley. For years visitors forced their way in and lit fires inside the tunnel, so two autumns ago the county council fitted a steel gate to protect the bats: upright bars, with gaps wide enough for a bat but too narrow for a person, above a solid steel panel. That January Brill counted 168 bats.

Ruth Okafor, the county ecologist, knew the gate had ended the fires, and she wondered what else it kept out. She spent her first evenings beside it with a bat detector, counting how many bats passed between the bars and how many turned away. She also weighed a few sleepers and hung temperature loggers along the tunnel.

The bats slipped through the gaps without slowing. The ones she weighed were far from thin despite the dry summer, fat enough to survive, and the loggers showed the warmest stretch of the tunnel as cold as ever. The answer was in the margins of Brill's notebooks, where he had always jotted his counts from the Fennick kilns, a roost visitors leave undisturbed. Twice before, the tunnel count had dropped by about a hundred while the kilns rose by the same amount, and both times the colony moved back within two winters. This January the kilns held 132 bats, against their usual thirty. The colony as a whole had suffered no fall; the missing bats had gone down the valley.

By then the council's working group had met four times, ordered drawings for a new gate with wider gaps, and issued a statement promising to protect the colony "whatever the cost." The bats had settled the kilns weeks before the first meeting, and Brill expects them home in a winter or two, by which time the drawings may be ready.
